summary: Lets a TLS server resume sessions without keeping per-client state. The server packs the session state into a ticket and hands it to the client, who can present it later to resume. It is a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 5077.

plainLanguage.summary: The server gives you a sealed coat-check ticket holding your details. Next time you show it, so the server need not remember you. A newer note replaced it.

questions: tls session resumption without server state
what is a tls session ticket
how does stateless session resumption work

subtitle: Lets servers avoid keeping TLS session state with client-held tickets.

tldr.problem: TLS servers usually keep per-client session state to enable fast session resumption, but this does not scale for servers handling many clients.
tldr.mechanism: The server encrypts and integrity-protects its session state into a ticket, sends it to the client during handshake, and the client presents it later to resume without the server keeping state.
tldr.outcome: This approach reduces server memory use and enables stateless session resumption, but was superseded by RFC 5077 which provides updates.

today: RFC 4507 was a Proposed Standard published in May 2006 and was obsoleted by RFC 5077. The session ticket mechanism remains widely used in TLS implementations as the primary method for stateless session resumption.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 4507 defines a way for TLS servers to resume sessions without keeping session-specific state for each client. Normally, when resuming a session, the TLS server must look up and recall the session state (such as the ciphersuite and master secret) from memory. This becomes problematic for servers handling a large number of transactions from different users, servers wanting to cache sessions for long periods, load-balanced systems, and embedded servers with limited memory.

The mechanism uses TLS extensions and a new TLS handshake message to distribute encrypted session-state information in the form of a ticket. The server creates the ticket and sends it to the client during a full handshake. The client can later present this ticket to resume the session without the server having retained any per-client state.
sections.plainLanguage: Big servers get tired of remembering every customer. So instead of the server keeping notes, it gives the customer a sealed envelope with their details inside. Next time the customer shows the envelope, the server opens it and knows who they are.

sections.title: Protocol Messages and Extensions
sections.content:
The specification defines two main components. The SessionTicket TLS extension is sent in ClientHello and ServerHello messages. When a client has a ticket, it includes it in the ClientHello; when it does not have one, it includes a zero-length extension to indicate willingness to receive a ticket. The server uses a zero-length extension in ServerHello to signal that it will send a new ticket.

The NewSessionTicket handshake message is sent by the server during a full handshake, after verifying the client's Finished message and before ChangeCipherSpec. This message carries the encrypted ticket and a ticket_lifetime_hint field indicating how long the client should store it. The ticket is opaque to the client; the client does not examine or modify it, only stores and presents it later.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer says "Do you have tickets?" in the greeting. The server says "Yes, I will give you one" and later hands over the sealed envelope.

sections.title: Session Resumption Flow
sections.content:
When resuming a session, the client sends the previously obtained ticket in the SessionTicket extension of a ClientHello. The server decrypts the ticket, verifies its validity, and retrieves the session state from its contents. If verification succeeds, the server may issue a new ticket and perform an abbreviated handshake. If the ticket is invalid, the server falls back to a full handshake.

The specification provides detailed message flows for four scenarios: issuing a new ticket during a full handshake, resuming with a previously issued ticket, completing a full handshake without issuing a ticket, and rejecting a ticket and performing a full handshake while issuing a new ticket.
sections.plainLanguage: Next time the customer comes back, they show the sealed envelope. The server opens it and checks if it is real. If it is, the customer gets right back to work quickly. If it is fake or broken, they start over from the beginning.

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content:
Tickets must be encrypted and authenticated to prevent modification or eavesdropping. The specification recommends using 128-bit AES in CBC mode for encryption and HMAC-SHA1 for integrity protection. A recommended ticket format includes a key identifier, initialization vector, encrypted state, and MAC. The state plaintext stores protocol version, ciphersuite, compression method, master secret, and client identity information.

Security considerations include invalidating sessions, protecting against stolen or forged tickets, and mitigating denial of service attacks. The key identifier in the ticket enables efficient rejection of old or unknown tickets. Keys must be managed carefully and changed regularly. Servers control ticket lifetime, and clients may have their own policy for discarding tickets. The mechanism preserves identity privacy by keeping ticket content confidential, though unlinkability is not guaranteed.
sections.plainLanguage: The server uses secret codes to seal and check the envelope so nobody can fake or change it. If the codes get old, the server stops accepting tickets made with them.

sections.title: Compatibility and History
sections.content:
RFC 4507 applies to TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and uses TLS extensions as defined in RFC 4366. The SessionTicket extension was assigned extension number 35, and the NewSessionTicket handshake message was assigned handshake type 4 by IANA. The mechanism is compatible with any TLS ciphersuite and may be used alongside the traditional session ID-based resumption.

The specification was obsoleted by RFC 5077, which provides clarifications and updates to the session ticket mechanism. Despite being superseded, the core concepts remain foundational to how modern TLS implementations handle stateless session resumption.
sections.plainLanguage: This way of doing tickets became the standard and is still used today. A newer update came along with small fixes, but the basic idea stayed the same.
